accuracy.evidence: Definitions of assumption, unconscious bias, confirmation bias and in-group bias checked against Nickerson (1998) and Tajfel (1970). The Tajfel description is kept to what the study showed (boys in trivially formed groups gave their own group more points), and the adult notes say that tests claiming to measure an individual's hidden bias are still debated, so nothing is overclaimed.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the real errors for this age: one quiet day is enough to judge (Kai prediction), seeing only what fits (bossy filter prediction and the Max late-days challenge), only unkind people or only adults have bias (challenge tags bad and adult), nice assumptions are harmless (glasses card in the sorter), and shame or hiding as the response (hide and shame tags).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagbias models a person's own judgement changing: a draggable friendliness guess with a ghost first-guess marker that moves as clues open, a filter that fades the actions that do not fit, a token split across random sticker teams, a flip panel that swaps the person, and a four-slot routine. The stereotype and prejudice labs sort groups and actions instead; the shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner experiences each bias before it is named: their first guess stays on the meter as a dashed line once the clues show Kai is shy and new; the noticing count reaches four that fit and four that do not; the token split is replayed back with the fact that the stickers were random; the flip panel shows why clothes say nothing about reading.

predictions.evidence: Two locked predictions with tempting wrong options: Kai is probably unfriendly (disproved when the four clues open), and you notice everything Mia does the same (disproved when the bossy filter leaves the kind actions faded until tapped).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating questions with ten tagged wrong answers (fact, evid, bad, adult, fair, memory, prove, agree, hide, shame). Each names the slip, for example that remembering 2 late days out of 12 is confirmation bias, or that asking who agrees with you is not evidence because others can share the same bias.

readability.evidence: Learner audience: kid text FK 2.6 against the 6.5 limit and adult text FK 7.3 against 9.5, from learn/readability.py. The key terms assumption, evidence, unconscious bias, confirmation bias, in-group bias and flip test are each defined in plain words the first time they appear.

no_filler.evidence: Filler gate clean and explanation overlap with Stereotypes and Prejudice lessons under the 12 percent limit. Kid paragraphs cover what bias is, first impressions, how bias grows and how to catch it; adult paragraphs give curriculum links, terms with sources, named mistakes and the lab tour.

mobile.evidence: iPhone 13 screenshots in dark and light for all six steps: the meter and four clue tiles fit at 390 px, Mia's eight actions sit in a 2 by 4 grid with readable text, the two token pots sit side by side and the order cards stack above four slots. phone_sweep reported 0 findings; walk.cjs passed on iPhone 13 and desktop.

accessibility.evidence: axe finds no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in either theme. The meter has Less friendly and Friendlier buttons, every action, token, flip, judgement and routine step has a button route, and the canvas aria-label and live region read each clue, tally and token split, so nothing depends on colour or dragging.
